name: South Route via Lake of the Angels
approach: From the Putvin Trailhead on Hamma Hamma River Road (FS 25, ~1,600 ft), the Putvin Trail (#813) is a steep, primitive trail, unmaintained in its upper reaches, that climbs steeply and directly from the start — expect root-staircase steps and a boot-track tread through forest for the first mile. About halfway up, the trail meets a rock headwall that requires hand-over-hand climbing; a large tree root serves as the key handhold, and on at least one especially steep pitch a fixed handline rope has historically been in place to assist. Above the headwall the trail eases into subalpine forest and heather meadows, passing near Whitehorse Basin and the Pond of the False Prophet before reaching Lake of the Angels (~4,850 ft) in a dramatic cirque below Mt. Stone's south face and the St. Peter's Gate notch — about 3 miles and roughly 3,000 ft of gain from the road. There is little to no reliable water on the lower trail; carry enough to reach the lake, and expect the trail to be slick when wet and to hold snow on shaded steps into early summer. From the lake, contour/climb toward St. Peter's Gate; just before the gate, turn sharply left (south) and traverse along the base of the cliffs to a notch in Mt. Stone's west ridge. Turn right at the notch and climb directly toward it, arriving at a first sub-summit rock; climb a short, low-Class-3 chimney to its top, cross a brief, somewhat exposed ridge to the base of the true summit spire, then follow a groove in the rock on the left side that bends right, where a faint climbers' path leads the last steps to the summit. The route is Class 3, with a few moves on the summit block that some parties rate Class 4; from Lake of the Angels camp, figure roughly 2.5 hours up to the summit.

approach_variants.name: Putvin Trail from Hamma Hamma Road to Lake of the Angels
camps: Hamma Hamma River road campgrounds — Lena Creek and Hamma Hamma
approach_variants.notes:
From the Putvin Trailhead on Hamma Hamma River Road (FS 25) at about 1,565-1,600 ft — an unmarked roadside pullout, roughly 4.5 miles past the Lena Lake Trailhead — the Putvin Trail is an unmaintained, primitive user trail that climbs steeply and directly from the first steps. Expect root-staircase steps and boot-track tread through forest for the first mile. In recent years a slide near road mile 10.5 has at times blocked the last 1.2 miles of road, adding a road-walk; check Forest Service status.

About halfway up the trail meets a rock headwall requiring hand-over-hand climbing, with a large tree root as the key handhold and, historically, a fixed handline on the steepest pitch. Above it the trail eases into subalpine forest and heather meadows, passing near Whitehorse Basin and the Pond of the False Prophet, and reaches Lake of the Angels at roughly 4,850-4,920 ft in a cirque below Mount Stone's south face — about 3 to 3.5 miles and 3,000 ft of gain. Little to no reliable water on the lower trail; carry enough to reach the lake.
approach_variants.season: Roughly Jun-Sep. Snow lingers in the basin above the lake well into summer
hazards: Trail-less, route-finding-dependent terrain above Lake of the Angels
Near-vertical root and rock steps on the lower Putvin Trail, genuinely exposed when wet, and worse descending on tired legs
Loose rock on the headwall and summit block with rockfall onto parties below
An ambiguous Class 3/4 crux near the summit
Fog is common here and multiple parties have lost the route on the upper mountain
approach_variants.baseFinding: The base of the climb is a notch in Mount Stone's west ridge, and the test for it is a turn you make before a gate. From Lake of the Angels contour and climb toward St. Peter's Gate — the obvious notch above the basin. Just before the gate, turn sharply left (south) and traverse along the base of the cliffs to a notch in the west ridge. If you walk through St. Peter's Gate, you have gone too far; the Gate is the marker you turn short of, not the one you pass through. That works in cloud because the cliff base is a tactile handrail: once you have made the turn, you keep rock on one side of you the whole traverse. Lose contact with the cliff and you have drifted downhill. Second test, at the notch: turn right and climb toward a first sub-summit rock, then up a short low class 3 chimney to its top. A chimney is a shape you can feel with both hands. If the first difficulty above the notch is a face or a slab rather than a chimney you can bridge, you are not on the line. Third test, on the summit spire: from the sub-summit cross a brief, somewhat exposed ridge to the base of the true summit spire, then follow a groove on the left side that bends right, where a faint climbers' path leads the last steps to the top. Left then right — a groove that runs straight up is not it. What the route's own timing says: about 2.5 hours up from the Lake of the Angels camp and about 1.5 hours back down. If you have been on the ground above the lake far longer than that without finding the notch, you have most likely missed the turn short of the Gate. Fog warning specific to this mountain: Mount Stone has more than one summit, and parties have confused the true south summit with the Middle and North summits in cloud. Count your ridges.

approach_variants.name: Lena Lake and Upper Lena Lake, the St. Peter's traverse from the east

bivy.name: Hamma Hamma River road campgrounds — Lena Creek and Hamma Hamma
bivy.notes: The drive-in staging option for everything on the Hamma Hamma side: Lena Lake and The Brothers, the Putvin trail to Lake of the Angels for Mount Skokomish and Mount Stone, and the Jefferson Creek spur for Mount Pershing. Lena Creek is the more useful of the two because it sits essentially at the Lena Lake trailhead, so a party arriving late can sleep at the car and start walking at first light instead of driving the gravel in the dark. This is a contingency and staging site rather than the normal plan for anyone climbing here — the objectives are all hours above it — but it is the right answer for a party that arrives after dark, gets weathered off, or comes out late and does not want to drive home tired. Being at 700 ft it is usable long before the high camps melt out, which makes it the practical base for an early-season Brothers attempt.
bivy.water: No potable water at either campground — this catches people out. The Hamma Hamma River runs alongside both and can be filtered, but bring drinking water from Hoodsport
bivy.permit: Modest per-night Forest Service fee with an extra vehicle charge, paid at the fee machine, which is cashless. No reservation system and no wilderness permit — this is developed Forest Service camping. Fire rings and picnic tables at each site, vault toilets, no hookups. Typically open from mid-May into late October and gated the rest of the year
bivy.capacity: Lena Creek has around thirteen well-spaced sites at the Lena Lake trailhead junction; Hamma Hamma has around fifteen a couple of miles further down the river. Both first come, first served, no reservations

approachLogistics.trailhead: Lena Lake Trailhead (Hamma Hamma Road, FR-25)

approach_variants.notes:
The other side of the same notch. From the Lena Lake Trailhead on FS 25 at roughly 600-750 ft, take the well-graded Lena Lake Trail #810 about 3 miles to Lena Lake at about 1,800 ft, then the steep primitive tread up the West Fork Lena Creek drainage roughly 3.5 more miles to Upper Lena Lake at about 4,550 ft, some 6.5 miles and 4,000 ft from the trailhead. Upper Lena Lake is the last maintained-trail camp and the last reliable water before the traverse goes cross-country; wilderness permit and bear canister required.

From Upper Lena Lake, leave the trail and head west on the Scout Lake way-trail across meadows and heather past Lena Tarn to Scout Pass at about 5,200 ft, down slightly to Upper Scout Lake, round it into Scout Basin, and up to Ullin's Pass at about 5,000 ft above the tarns known as Ullin's Bathtubs. From there a rising traverse above the small lakes leads to a snow ramp across a steep hillside below Mount Stone that ends at a loose moraine, and then exposed dirt-and-mud slopes to St. Peter's Gate at about 5,950 ft.

This is a two- or three-day trip and it is chosen for the country it crosses, not because it is quicker.
approach_variants.season: Roughly Jul-Sep, once the off-trail benches and passes are largely clear
hazards: Extensive off-trail way-trail route-finding over multiple passes and basins with faint tread
Loose glacial moraine of all sizes near St. Peter's Gate and exposed dirt-and-mud slopes on the final ramp
Fog on the upper mountain — multiple parties have lost the route here and ended up in harder terrain
No dependable water between Upper Lena Lake and the tarns near Ullin's Pass
A very long approach with limited bail options partway through
approach_variants.baseFinding: Coming from the east you arrive at St. Peter's Gate itself, which is the high point of the traverse at about 5,950 ft and an obvious rocky notch in Mount Stone's southeast ridge. That is the arrival test and it is unmistakable in any weather: the ground stops rising, the notch pinches, and the Lake of the Angels basin opens on the far side. From the gate there are two ways onto the peak and they are different climbs. The one this route describes is the west-ridge notch: go through the Gate and drop toward the Lake of the Angels basin, then work back up and turn the corner onto the cliff-base traverse to the notch in the west ridge — the same notch the Putvin parties reach by turning sharply left just short of the Gate. The other is the south-face gully, which starts by descending about 300 ft from the Gate to the base of a basalt cliff; that is the Lena Lake traverse route's line, not this one. So the fog test for this variant is which side of the gate you end up on: this route goes over to the Lake of the Angels side and approaches the west ridge from the south-west, keeping the cliff base at your shoulder. Above the notch the tests are identical to the Putvin variant: turn right, low Class 3 chimney to a sub-summit, a brief exposed ridge, then a groove on the left that bends right to the true south summit.

pitch_detail.notes: An unmaintained, very steep climbers' trail from Hamma Hamma River Road that climbs roughly 3,000 ft in about 3 miles to Lake of the Angels. Carry water: the lower trail is largely dry, and roots and steps are slick when wet.

Midway up, the trail meets a rock headwall climbed hand over hand on roots, sometimes with a fixed handline. Above it a climbers' path leads to a small meadow near 4,400 ft. Downclimb it facing in on the way out.
Continue north from the meadow and the lake toward St. Peter's Gate, the notch in the ridge above the basin. This ground can stay snow-covered into summer.

Just before the Gate, turn sharply left (south) and traverse along the base of the cliffs to a notch in the west ridge. Parties who lose the faint path here are drawn up into steeper Class 3–4 gullies on the south face; stay with the cliff base.

Turn right at the notch and scramble a couple of hundred feet to a first sub-summit, finishing up a short low-Class-3 chimney. Beyond it, a shallow hanging basin with a small lingering snowfield leads across toward the summit block.

A short, somewhat exposed ridge reaches the base of the summit spire. Climb the groove on its left side, which bends right, then a faint path to the top; the rock is solid pillow basalt, with a few Class 4 moves reported. Reverse the same line to descend.

climbing_route.label: Traverse to the west-ridge notch
climbing_route.notes: From Lake of the Angels contour/climb toward St. Peter's Gate; just before the gate, turn sharply left (south) and traverse along the base of the cliffs to a notch in Mt. Stone's west ridge.

climbing_route.label: Chimney to the first sub-summit
climbing_route.notes: Turn right at the notch and climb directly toward it, arriving at a first sub-summit rock; climb a short, low-Class-3 chimney to its top.

climbing_route.label: Exposed ridge to the summit spire
climbing_route.notes: Cross a brief, somewhat exposed ridge to the base of the true summit spire.

climbing_route.label: Groove on the left side to the summit
climbing_route.notes: Follow a groove in the rock on the left side that bends right, where a faint climbers' path leads the last steps to the summit. The route is Class 3, with a few moves on the summit block that some parties rate Class 4; figure roughly 2.5 hours up from Lake of the Angels camp.
